analysis.one_liner: Expands federal compensation for sick uranium miners, millers, ore haulers, and Navajo downwinders.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: the Senate Judiciary Committee held one hearing on it in October 1998, then the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 with no committee vote and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the 1990 Radiation Exposure Compensation Act, which pays people harmed by the government's nuclear weapons program. It would have added parts of the Navajo Nation hit by Nevada test fallout, covered uranium millers, aboveground and open-pit miners, and ore transporters (not just underground miners), raised payments to $200,000, loosened strict eligibility rules like the smoker distinction, and added diseases such as colon, brain, bladder, and breast cancer. It also would have paid $50,000 to workers secretly used in federal radiation experiments and made it easier for Native American claimants to file.
analysis.who_benefits: Former uranium miners, millers, and ore transport workers who developed cancer or lung disease, their survivors, residents of the Navajo Nation exposed to Nevada test fallout, and victims of undisclosed federal radiation experiments. The bill raised the standard payment to $200,000, cut the required radiation exposure in half (to 40 working level months), extended the covered years to 1942-1990, dropped eligibility penalties for smoking or drinking, and directed that any doubt about a claim be resolved in the claimant's favor, with the claim automatically granted if the Attorney General did not decide within 12 months [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sick uranium workers and Navajo downwinders

how_it_helps.text: Adds the fallout-affected parts of the Navajo Nation Reservation in Arizona, Utah, and New Mexico to the list of 'affected areas' eligible for downwinder compensation.

Extends uranium-worker compensation beyond underground miners to people who milled uranium, worked aboveground or open-pit mines, or transported ore, and to any state where that work happened, not just the originally listed states.

Raises the payment to $200,000 per claim, lowers the required radiation exposure to 40 working level months, shortens the required work history to one year, and extends the covered employment window from 1947-1971 to 1942-1990.

Drops eligibility restrictions that penalized claimants for smoking, drinking, coffee consumption, or their age at first exposure, and adds compensable diseases including male and female breast cancer, colon, brain, ovarian, bladder, and salivary gland cancers, and chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Creates a $50,000 payment for uranium workers who were, without their knowledge or consent, intentionally exposed to radiation in federal research, and a $20,000 payment for workers injured on the job who were barred from workers' compensation or civil suits available to other miners.

Rewrites claim procedures in workers' favor: all reasonable doubt resolved for the claimant, affidavits and Indian Health Service or VA diagnoses treated as conclusive evidence, a claim deemed awarded if the Attorney General misses the 12-month deadline, and attorney's fees and 8% interest paid by the government when a denial is overturned in court.

Directs the Attorney General to respect Native American law and custom in processing claims, use ethnic-specific lung-function standards, and, at a tribe's request, contract with tribal organizations to administer claims for tribal members under the Indian Self-Determination Act.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, through the taxpayer-funded Radiation Exposure Compensation trust fund. The bill placed no new liability on the mining and milling companies that employed the workers; restitution for work done 'for the use and benefit of the United States Government' would come from the Treasury, at $200,000 per qualifying cancer or lung-disease claim plus $50,000 and $20,000 awards under the new provisions [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers through the claims fund

drawbacks.text: The bill is expensive and open-ended: it raises the standard award to $200,000, extends coverage to any state where uranium was moved, stretches the covered period to 1942-1990, and compensates 'any other medical condition associated with uranium mining, milling, or transport,' language broad enough to make total cost to the trust fund hard to predict.

Even for supporters, the payments are partial restitution: a lump sum cannot restore health, and the bill itself requires a follow-up federal report on whether people near uranium mills and tailings actually have access to adequate medical care, an admission that money alone does not fix the health problem.

The bill amends a compensation program administered by the Justice Department, and it gives the Attorney General major new gatekeeping duties (audits of x-ray readings, revised regulations within 180 days) without spelling out the funding for that administration, a gap critics of program expansion typically raised.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the affected workers and their families the benefit is concrete and large: cash restitution for cancers and lung disease caused by work the federal government knowingly left unsafe, plus far easier qualification than the 1990 law allowed. The cost falls on the general Treasury, and the bill's broad definitions make the total outlay uncertain; an honest supporter would concede that 'any condition associated with uranium mining' is written loosely and would likely have needed tightening. But the bill's own findings describe the 1990 program as slower and stricter for uranium workers than for other compensated groups, so the expansion was aimed at a documented failure, not a speculative one [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee, which held a single hearing in October 1998, but the committee never voted it out and the full Senate never voted on it before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Bingaman of New Mexico introduced the bill on July 22, 1998, with one Democratic cosponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.

The bill's findings argued that the 1990 compensation law had failed uranium workers, who faced stricter criteria and slower payment than other compensated groups, and cited a Senate Labor and Human Resources oversight hearing and the President's Advisory Committee on Human Radiation Experiments in support of the changes.
On October 7, 1998, the Judiciary Committee held a hearing on the bill, its only recorded action beyond referral.
No committee vote, no Senate floor vote, and no House action followed; the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury came out ahead, avoiding the expanded $200,000-per-claim payouts and new award categories; the uranium workers, their survivors, and Navajo Nation residents the bill would have paid gained nothing from this bill, and the Justice Department avoided rewriting its claims procedures.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators, both Democrats, put their names on the bill, and no vote was ever taken, so there is no record of who would have supported or opposed it.

industries.note: The bill's payouts ($200,000 per qualifying claim, plus $50,000 and $20,000 awards and attorney's fees and interest when denials are overturned) come from the federal claims fund, so the general taxpayer bears the cost. The bill's premise is that the government itself failed to warn and protect uranium workers, so paying is restitution for the government's own conduct.

industries.industry: Uranium mining, milling, and transport companies
industries.note: The bill imposes no new liability on the companies that employed the sickened workers; the employers' role in exposing workers to radon and other hazards goes unaddressed, and compensation flows entirely from the federal government instead. The bill does mandate a federal report on reclamation of mines, mills, and tailings in five states, but recommends no enforcement against industry.

industries.industry: Nuclear weapons complex legacy liabilities (Energy Department and its contractors)
industries.note: The bill would have expanded public acknowledgment and payment for harms from the weapons program, including a $50,000 award for workers secretly used in radiation experiments, and required the Energy Department to help produce a report on mill tailings and reclamation. It creates no new cleanup mandate, only reporting and recommendations.
